extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, critics, and advanced creative writers studying narrative theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic guidance and evaluative criteria for describing and producing narrative effects (point of view, narratorial authority, reader relation, temporal devices) with frequent reference to Proust and the novel. Useful for critics and writers assessing or designing novelistic discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auctorial discourse (authorial commentary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proliferation of an 'auctorial' discourse indicates both the presence of the author (actual or fictive) and a sovereign authority in the work; when commentary invades the story it can transform the novel into an essay and disrupt traditional novelistic equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the quantity and quality of authorial/ideological commentary and its effects: e.g., Tolstoy, Mann, Broch, Malraux transfer commentary onto characters; Proust concentrates it in Marcel/the narrator. Excessive intellectualizing can shock the novel's form (positive or negative effect). Anti-pattern: turning a narrative into an intellectual treatise that substitutes speculation for embodied action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narratee location and diegetic level
rubrics_metrics.description: The narratee is an element of the narrating situation and is necessarily located on the same diegetic level as the narrator: an intradiegetic narrator implies an intradiegetic narratee; an extradiegetic narrator addresses an extradiegetic narratee (often merging with the implied reader).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the narratee is intradiegetic (creates distance and interposition between narrator and real reader) or extradiegetic (increases transparency and identification with implied reader). Examples: epistolary 'second-person' marks address an intradiegetic correspondent; Sterne or Balzac sometimes signal provincial vs Parisian implied readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied reader's role and readerly liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives presuppose an implied reader who is entrusted not only with 'guessing' the work's structures but with interpreting and reintegrating them; the author should allow readers liberty to translate the universe of the work into their own terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how a text recruits or permits readerly interpretation and production. Proust's explicit injunction: 'the author must not be indignant' when readers read 'in their own particular fashion.' Good practice: design texts that invite readers to reinterpret and re-encode significance rather than forcing a single meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between narrator and author
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator (fictive speaking instance) does not necessarily merge with the real author; lapses or intrusions of the 'author' must be distinguished from the narrator's voice and functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or creating narrative voice, avoid conflating narrator opinions with author's intent. Note functions of narrator (commentary, custody of truth, ideological authority) separately from biographical authorial claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analytic categories as provisional tools, not a canon
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts and procedures (prolepses, analepses, iterative, focalizations, paralipses, metadiegetic, etc.) are instruments for description and discovery, not immutable laws; they will date and should not be hypostatized into a 'Canon.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these categories diagnostically and empirically; be wary of over-systematizing or reifying them. The grid is a 'procedure of discovery'—use it to reveal features (e.g., iterative narrative, pseudo-diegetic instances) but keep methodological humility and openness to revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist forced unity and teleological closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not seek unity at any price or force interpretative rhetoric that makes a heterogeneous, historically contingent work appear artificially coherent; restore and respect a work's sense of unfulfillment, contingency, and indefiniteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether critical or creative attempts to impose final synthesis are masking material heterogeneity or historical contingency (e.g., war, death) that shaped the work. Good practice: allow retroactive, belated unity to be acknowledged rather than explained away as original design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileging originality and the 'writerly' text
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a critical/petitician preference for the 'writerly' (modern) over the 'readerly' (classical); the literary goal can be to transform the reader from consumer into producer of the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or creating work, consider whether the text invites active reader production (ambiguity, participatory structures, unconventional devices). Valorizing innovation is a legitimate stance but is also a critic's bias—make this preference explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage narratorial ideological authority
rubrics_metrics.description: In some works the narrator holds a privileged position of ideological commentary that few characters may contest; this dominance shapes the work's tone and interpretive economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess (or design) how much interpretive authority the narrator claims and whether other voices are permitted to contest it. Anti-pattern: allowing the narrator to monopolize truth so that characters become mere mouthpieces or the work becomes dogmatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be observed, not merely mouthpieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters ought not to function primarily as organs of authorized speculative discourse; their errors, absurdities, failures, and silent teachings (e.g., through action or art) are often more instructive than their expressed opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dramatized showing—character actions, failures, and silences—over expository dialogue that turns figures into didactic spokesmen. Example: Proust's characters (Swann, Charlus, Bergotte) are objects of observation rather than custodians of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat reader as potential co-author (narratee as real author)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'real author' of a narrative is sometimes as much the one who hears it as the one who tells it; narratives that invite the reader to 'rewrite' the text (Pierre Menard effect) mobilize the narratee as co-creator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design interpretive gaps, echoes, or structural invites that allow readers to recombine or re-create meaning. Evaluate how explicitly a text encourages such rewriting (Proust-Borges-Pier re Menard anecdote is given as emblematic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge retroactivity and material contingency in composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative coherence may be 'retroactive'—unity won belatedly over heterogeneous material—and expansion or structure can be the result of contingent historical events (e.g., war, death), not solely deliberate composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In criticism avoid teleological explanations that ascribe present structure to original plan; in creative practice, be aware that composition may legitimately incorporate later accretions and heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer empirical, partial 'laws' and remain self-critical
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of narrative (as formulated) are partial, defective, and empirical; the critic/poetician should expect their own schemes to decay and be revised over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep methodological modesty: present categories as working hypotheses. Beware of 'the semiotic universe abhors a vacuum'—naming contingency already assigns it function; critics should avoid speaking 'too much' in finalizing ways.
